hints: Focus on what type of compound actually reacts with HCN, and what the new product looks like.
Remember HCN adds across the C=O of aldehydes and ketones to give R2C(OH)(CN), so draw the product carbon for each carbonyl compound.
Check which product carbon ends up with four different groups attached, as that is the test for a chiral centre.
walkthrough:
**Recall the HCN addition reaction**

Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN to form cyanohydrins. The carbonyl carbon becomes a new carbon bonded to OH and CN.

General equation:
$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)}$$

**Apply the test for chirality**

A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups attached. So we need the starting carbonyl to give a product where the new C(OH)(CN) carbon has four different substituents.

**Test the aldehyde ethanal**

For $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$, addition gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)(CN)}$.

Look at the central carbon: it is bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$. That is four different groups, so it is chiral. This fits the question perfectly.

options.A: CH3CHO + HCN gives CH3CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile). The carbon is attached to H, CH3, OH and CN, four different groups, so it is a chiral centre.
options.B: CH3CH2COCH2CH3 is pentan-3-one, a symmetrical ketone. Its cyanohydrin is CH3CH2C(OH)(CN)CH2CH3, where the central carbon has two identical ethyl groups, so it cannot be chiral.
options.C: CH3CO2CH3 is an ester, methyl ethanoate. Esters do not undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN like aldehydes and ketones do, so no cyanohydrin is formed.
options.D: HCHO is methanal. Its cyanohydrin is HOCH2CN, where the carbon has two identical H atoms plus OH and CN, so it has only three types of group and is achiral.
